correctness.rationale: The quantity is a relative squared residual in the stated product probability measure, not its square root or a residual on direction-dependent intervals. The section pulls back via Q^(1/2) to a ball section of squared radius 1−t²/(uᵀQu); the area multiplier is det(Q^(1/2))/||Q^(1/2)u|| by the plane cofactor formula, and continuity gives the possible tangent endpoints. The normalized kernel is f(u)−s²g(u) with f=q^(−1/2), g=q^(−3/2). In the orthonormal offset basis 1, (s²−1/3)/√(4/45), its two columns are f−g/3 and −√(4/45)g. Their Gram matrix has trace S=||F||²>0 and determinant (4/45)D. The best rank-one fit captures the top eigenvalue by maximizing over the offset factor of unit norm; arbitrary offset factors outside the two-dimensional span cannot improve it. Hence the smaller root divided by S is the claimed error, and Cauchy–Schwarz makes D zero only for q constant; continuity and polarization give Q scalar. For the local expansion use D=m_1² Var_w(q^(−1)), where w is probability density q^(−1)/m_1 relative to spherical measure. Uniformly q=1+ε(uᵀBu−c)+O(ε²), with c the least eigenvalue of B for ε>0 and greatest for ε<0. Since the variance removes the constant c and w converges uniformly to 1, D=ε² Var(uᵀBu)+o(ε²). The fourth moments yield variance (2/15)||B−tr(B)I/3||_F²; S→8/15 and the smaller-root expansion has coefficient (4/45)/(8/15)²=5/16 multiplying D, giving 1/24. For both axial families q(z)=A+Bz² and z is uniform on [0,1] after folding. Integration of (z q^(1−j))' gives (3−2j)m_{j−1}+2(j−1)A m_j=q(1)^(1−j), establishing both recurrences for j=2,3; direct integration gives the arctan and arcosh first moments. The prolate rescaling y=Lz is dominated, for L≥√2, by (1+y²/2)^(−j); the limits of Lm_j are π/2, π/4, 3π/16. Thus LS→89π/240 and L²D→π²/32. For the oblate family the recurrences give L²m_1∼log(2L), L²m_2→1/2 and L²m_3→1/4; the leading term of D is log(2L)/(4L⁴). This yields both the positive prolate limit and the oblate 1/(45 log L) asymptotic. The latter invalidates any bound on eccentricity based on uniformly small defect in this sampling model.
residual_risks: Packaged checker inspected, not executed. Its geometry loop enumerates 4×69=276 area comparisons, not the 280 reported in VERIFICATION.md. This is a count discrepancy, not a defect in the analytic proof.

Exact check replay: for the prolate ratio L=√2 integrate (1+z²)^(−j) over [0,1]; one gets (π/4, π/8+1/4, 3π/32+1/4). Insert these into the trace and determinant of the orthonormal-offset Gram matrix above. The asymptotic proof uses the uniform expansion and dominated convergence, not this finite example.

The phrase positive derivative near the end of the near-ball proof refers to the quadratic response. The ordinary first derivative at the ball is zero. The claimed coefficient and null-space for the quadratic term are correct; scalar first-order perturbations can still have anisotropic higher-order terms.

value.rationale: Finite separability prompts a natural quantitative question: how informative is one separated fit for a nonspherical ellipsoid? The answer distinguishes exact rigidity, local sensitivity, and a sharp obstruction to reading eccentricity from fit quality. The same axis ratio can produce a defect bounded away from zero or an error asymptotically vanishing at a quantified logarithmic rate. This is a meaningful contrast for interpreting a separability statistic and is not a reformulation of rank two or of the customary ellipsoid-section formula.
residual_risks: The interpretation depends on the stated relative squared L² norm and common-offset sampling; no geometric stability for arbitrary bodies or arbitrary anisotropic degenerations follows.
